title: We want to retire early in Malaysia on rental income. Cash or leverage?
excerpt: A British family in Singapore with RM3 million plans to retire early in Kuala Lumpur on rental income. Sean explains the foreign-buyer minimums and why he'd rent first and use some leverage.

question.asker: From D, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: D, 47, and his wife, who grew up in Penang, are British and rent in Singapore, where he works; they have two teenagers. They have about RM3 million in cash, UK buy-to-let homes bringing in about £20,000 a year with small mortgages, and shares. In a few years D wants to retire early to Kuala Lumpur, owning a home to live in and several rental units, and eventually pass them to the children.
question.text: Are fees the same for foreign buyers, should they buy three properties in cash or more with loans, and which areas suit them?

answer.quote: Property investment is a wealth diversification tool, not a money making tool.
answer.summary: Don't tie all the cash up in three unleveraged properties. Rent for six to twelve months first, settle on the school and the area, buy your own home, then add investment units one at a time, putting down 20% to 30% so each one's rent covers its instalment. Focus on quality, not the number of properties.

reasons.title: Foreign buyers face minimum prices
reasons.body: Sean says the minimum for foreigners is RM1 million in Kuala Lumpur and RM2 million in most of Selangor, with zones and exceptions, and foreigners can't buy individual-title landed homes. He says stamp duty is the same as for locals, and Singapore-based salaried staff get loans easily.

reasons.title: Property protects wealth, tenants build it
reasons.body: A RM500,000 unit worth RM1.2 million in 30 years mostly keeps pace with inflation. The real gain is the tenant paying off the loan, leaving a fully owned property.

reasons.title: Expat areas cost expat prices
reasons.body: Mont Kiara, Bangsar and Damansara Heights suit investment because expats pay high rents, but living just a street away in Segambut, Sri Damansara or Kota Damansara can cut rent by 30% to 40%. For a retired couple, Shah Alam, Subang Jaya, Penang or Ipoh offer even more for the money.

reasons.title: Malaysia rewards homework, not certainty
reasons.body: Unlike Singapore or the UK, Kuala Lumpur sees 20 or more launches a month, so not every unit makes money. Choosing units whose rent covers the instalment, through subsales, auctions or bulk purchases, matters more than the count.

actions: Rent for six to twelve months and spend weekends exploring areas before buying.
Choose your younger child's school first, since it will decide where you live.
Check the foreign-buyer minimum price for each zone and state before shortlisting.
At about 50 you may get loans of around 20 years; put down enough that the rent covers each instalment.
Compare new launches, subsales, auctions and bulk purchases before buying each investment unit.
caveat: Foreign-ownership rules can change and are often announced before they take effect, so confirm the current thresholds with a lawyer. If convenience matters more than value, living in the expat areas is still a reasonable choice.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #216. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures and rules are as Sean stated them in July 2023. Sean mentions a conversation with the founder of FAR Capital, a property investment club he is a client of.
